Sometimes it’s hard to explain to people what racism looks & feels like. 

What it’s like to walk into a 350 room hotel in Cannes with many (white) people coming/going & be the only person stopped before entering, questioned if I have a room here. 
Lemme tell u the feeling sucks

And when I calmly raised my concerns with reception that I have been singled out/profiled because I am not-white, the receptionist doubles down, asks if I AM in fact staying at the hotel, defends the bellman/security, says they don’t know me (but know the 100s they didn’t stop?)
I’ve had a week of nothing but terrific service experiences in France. I am devastated this happened.

When you’re a person of colour, you just know in your bones when you’ve experienced racism, yet it’s hard to prove. You learn to ignore it and deal. But sometimes it just smacks you in the face that you can’t.

And I recognise this racist micro aggression at a stupid luxury hotel is nothing compared to what Black, Indigenous, dark skinned POC experience daily, where jogging, wearing a hoodie, not pulling over fast enough can mean death.

You learn you always have to be presentable so you don’t get singled out. You learn to dress up to do an errand or, say, go to a car dealership. I’ve spent too much time trying to make a good impression just so I won’t be judged. It’s exhausting. And sometimes still doesn’t work.

I generally crave being ignored/unbothered in public. I’m tweeting this to remind myself that it is tied to privilege. Because when you aren’t the dominant caste, they will question your right to be in their space (like a Black man bird watching in Central Park).

@cindyisAWOL Not really helpful (from a relatively rich caucasian living in a relatively free country who is pretty much free to travel the world that is) but there is always someone in a worse position.

@bcleeve You’re right, not really helpful :/ 

“Keep a stiff upper lip, many have it worse” is something that was ingrained into me by my immigrant parents; it’s the way they survived in a new country. It’s taken years of travel, writing & self exploration to strip that toxic attitude.
@cindyisAWOL Apologies.  Didn't mean to offend or belittle the effect of racism/tribalism on you.

I'm on sabbatical this year, which I really needed after 3 semesters of teaching during COVID. But today has brought back a lot of that burnout and I'd like to tell you about it. 1/

I think one of the traits that makes me a good prof is that I remember my own struggles as an undergrad v well. @uchicago, my alma matter, is not known as a gentle place! I try to grant my students understanding and kindness that I would have benefited from 2/

Obviously, since Spring 2020, it's been hard to be a human and focusing on college coursework has been tough. Students were getting sick, their families were sick, they were trying to work in a pandemic, often supporting families, they had major financial insecurities 3/
And I don't know about you my my focus has SUFFERED and it did for plenty of them, too. So I did everything I could to help. 4/

I removed all the late penalties. I know some students wouldn't have made it without this. But it's risky. Many students put off all the work until the end of term, don't master the basics, then try to do it all at once without a foundation. Grading comes in a tidal wave 5/

It made my job a lot harder in a lot of ways. Some students appreciated it. Some docked me in evaluations because they said the couldn't work "without deadlines". (we had deadlines, just no punishments for missing them, so I guess they can't work without punishment?) 6/

And for students who still couldn't get it done, I granted incompletes to anyone who asked. This gives you ~6 more months to finish the work. It is meant for students who have done the majority of the work but like, end up in the hospital and just can't finish on time. 7/

They are supposed to be rare and at the professor's discretion. I let everyone have one who was failing - ENCOURAGED it, in fact - and I think I gave out about 25 of them in the spring semester.  That work is all due today 8/

About 5 students finished the work earlier this year. The rest are trying to finish it today. For many, it's half a semester's worth of work, including the midterm and final, because they couldn't/didn't work on it until this week. 9/

They are having all those troubles I mentioned - they can't use some of the tools we learned in the 2nd week because they didn't do it in the 2nd week and now are trying to do work that requires the mastery they would have gained over 15 weeks 10/

I feel bad for them. I know there is life outside of class and how hard it has been to get things done and how hard it is to independently do this coursework. I'm spending all day on line answering questions and helping them through 11/

BUT GODDAM IF THERE AREN'T STUDENTS BICKERING OVER INDIVIDUAL POINTS TODAY

BICKERING OVER POINTS IS ONE OF THE CURSES OF BEING A PROFESSOR 

12/

I was never a point begger, so I wonder if these students realize that they're not just gaming a system that impacts their GPA but that they are telling an actual human being that they did their job poorly. A human who has broken every rule to help them avoid an F in this case
13

I'm not accepting any comments about the pressure on students about GPAs and all of this. I've been in universities since I was 18 and promise I know how it works and what student life is like better than you do. 
14/

@jengolbeck Honestly, as a grad student right now. I feel like you probably have fallen into the trap of being too accommodating. It sounds like you really care, but maybe try to care a little less? Strict deadlines are actually helpful to many.
@ExilePasta Well, I've been teaching university courses since 1999, so I feel like I'm cool with my system

Please read this thread if you are considering tweeting offensive or otherwise problematic things you believe are self-evidently “irony” or “sarcasm”

It will not work. It will not land. It will not matter years later when people see those tweets “out of context.”

This is why.

In the real world, with people who know us, sometimes we might say outrageous things which get big laughs precisely *because* our friends know there is a deliberate comic disconnect between who they know us to be & the wacky edgy statement we just served up with the hot wings.

For example, among my closest female friends, I might say something like “Ha ha women are the worst, am I right?”

And they laugh because they know I am a woman & an outspoken feminist, so the only reason I’d say that to them would be to mock that pervasive cultural assumption

We see people make a lot of trouble for themselves with tweets they claim are clearly ironic.

Some of that is just PR & they really are racist misogynist sacks of crap.

But some of it comes from not understanding how to codeshift between in-group discourse & public discourse.

A lot of people got positive feedback making “edgy” jokes to their friends who know they don’t mean it & are setting up ironic juxtaposition

But on the internet, bitch we don’t know you.

We don’t know the “context” is just supposed to be that you’re a super good dude, acksually

It’s one thing to joke “women are the worst” among my friends in response to whatever sexist bullshit happened to one of us.

If I just tweet “Women are the worst” there is no way at all for anyone to know I’m not serious & referencing some movie or situation. You don’t know me.

And it really, really doesn’t work years down the line when my kid can’t open a can of beans & someone goes through my tweets & finds “women are the worst” sitting there like an old dry turd.

Any context is long opaque. Any irony based on you knowing me is a HUGE assumption.

Every dumbass own-goal tweet gets called satire or irony or out of context.

This does not work on Twitter especially without explicit quote-tweeting, including any context in the tweet, & even then probably sOmE cRaP LiKe ThIs to make double sure

(Or hey just don’t tweet it)

I think part of why it’s often (not always) public figures belonging to certain demographics that get caught with a bunch of “edgy” tweets is that said demographic doesn’t have to code shift as much in real life as others & are accustomed to people assuming their good intent.

They genuinely believe they are so self-evidently a good, funny, moral person that any offensive thing they say will be intrinsically understood to be top comedy.

Their friends always get it. What the internet’s fucking problem?

The Internet’s problem is the context & irony was based on everyone knowing you & knowing how great you are at heart, so any bad thing you say must be ironic by definition.

But it’s just words on a screen, man. There’s no hot new check mark denoting a good person & thus irony.

I notice a lot of these old tweets come from the early 2010s as well—a time when shifting between social interaction IRL & online was still something everyone was working out on their own amid a lot of “the internet isn’t real life” misguided advice.

Ultimately, no one cares if you were being ironic & assuming everyone knew you were super cool so it’s ok.

All they see is your goddamned tweet full of slurs, which you chose to put into the world & slap your name on, & they’re not interested in knowing you at all.

And that’s if you are indeed simply confused about the definitions of “irony” & “satire” & not just a standard internet dickosaurus.

Because I got news for you: there’s no way for us to tell the difference. It’s all the same words & tone as the real thing.

So maybe ask yourself, before you tweet your rad dark edgy joke you think is irony with a rich & clear context:

Is the context just that it’s absurd that anyone would think I actually believe this?

Why do I think the entire goddamned Internet knows & likes me that much?

Perhaps consider that the use of actual fucking slurs means that you are not only putting brutal ugliness into the world for very little purpose & making yourself look indistinguishable from bigots, but that it makes it trivially easy to find the worst things you’ve ever said.

In conclusion, if you post shit you don’t mean we are not your bar buddies & we have no reason to believe you aren’t 100% sincere.

Maybe a bunch of offensive words on their own without commentary isn’t as funny as you think, & your beautiful soul is not public knowledge.

• What Is RECURRENT MISCARRIAGE?
Let's breakdown the phrase...

RECURRENT: Something occurring repeatedly
MISCARIAGE: The loss of pregnancy before the 20th week of pregnancy.

"It's the repeated loss of a confirmed pregnancy before the 20th week of pregnancy" https://t.co/5EcCjcourz

• What Are The Causes?
1. GENETICS
- Every fertilized egg gets 23 chromosomes from each parent. There are times it could be more or less making it abnormal.

-The body tries to eliminates it because it's abnormal and this causes 60% of miscarriages and it's common in older women https://t.co/np7JUDBykV

2. RHESUS FACTOR INCOMPATIBILITY

- When the blood of the mother is Rh-ve and the baby blood is Rh+ve.

- There is a difference in the Rh factor between a mother(-) and the baby(+), the body of the mother recognizes the baby as a foreign body, attacks it and causes a miscarriage. https://t.co/GOqaXcgOVl

3. HORMONAL IMBALANCE
- Progesterone is the hormone of pregnancy, the hormone that keeps the baby till birth. 

- Any condition that raises or reduces this hormone will cause a miscarriage.

4. UTERINE STRUCTURE ABNORMALITY
- The uterus commonly known as the womb houses the child https://t.co/FeJgjYbkNF

anything that affects the space where the unborn baby is supposed to implant itself in the womb such as FIBROID can cause miscarriage. 

The cervix that is the gate of the womb sometimes is too weak and doesn't close (INCOMPETENT CERVIX) and this can also cause miscarriage. https://t.co/YoyzO4me5G

5. INFECTIONS
- Infections such as Rubella (German Measles), Herpes Simplex, Chlamydia can affect baby growth and cause miscarriage.

6. SMOKING
- People who smoke weed/tobacco and take alcohol in pregnancy are at risk of having miscarriage because these things affect the child. https://t.co/4UEYNvG2w8

I was born & raised in rural/Northern Ontario. 
I've done work to end violence against women for 17 yrs.

Some quick facts you should know about violence against women in a rural Canadian context:

1- Guns. Guns. Guns.

I grew up in a house of guns and I literally did not know a single person growing up who did not have guns in their house.

Domestic violence gets cranked up to 11 when you know the man has access to a firearm.

2- Confidentiality is largely a joke.

Everyone knows everyone. Everyone knows you. Everyone knows your abuser. 

The officer assigned to your case might be the same guy who busted you for underage drinking when you were 15.

3- Resources are limited or non existent.

Shelters that might be hours away from your house, limited beds, long wait times, etc. 

Because funding from government is on a per capita basis, fewer people = less money, even though the cost-per-victim is actually higher.

4- Poverty, poverty, poverty.

Because Canada has shifted to an urban country, the youth migration, dying of old industries, etc. has meant that most rural communities have incredibly high levels of poverty and often, intense dichotomies with no real middle class.

5- Limited transportation options.

If you don't have a car and money to gas it up, you're screwed in a rural context. Public transit is non-existent or extremely limited.

6- The few resources that do exist, have massive catchment areas.

For example, the sexual assault centre in Renfrew County has a catchment area the size of Prince Edward Island.

Which means it's actually long distance to call from one end of the county to another. It's HUGE.

Add all these obstacles in an already difficult situation and we can't be surprised by what happened in Wilno in 2015 or what happened in Nova Scotia earlier this year.

Rural women face so many barriers to a life of safety and I desperately want urban feminists to pay attention.

@JulieSLalonde I don’t mean to try and tell you your business but number 7 would have to be social stigma/pressures. Women in small town where everyone knows everyone are under tremendous social pressure & judgement every day.

Music Streaming as an Economic Shift (a theory in 8 tweets):

1/8. Economically speaking, streaming services take a lower cut (~30%) than download stores (~35%) or CD manufacturers/distributors/sellers (~55%), and thus are better for artists (and the rest of the music industry) per $ spent.
2/8. Streaming is also now producing more total $ than downloads ever did, and is on track to MAYBE generate more inflation-adjusted royalties than CDs within a couple years.

3/8. Those $, however, are distributed differently across listeners. In the CD era, the highest spenders each controlled $1000s/year of buying. In the streaming era, they control $10/month at most, like anybody else.

4/8. The argument over pro-rata and user-centric payment models SOUNDS like it's about this, but the (current) pro-rata streaming model is actually biased TOWARDS smaller artists, in practice, by a small (5-10%) amount.
5/8. The people who listen more, and thus control more $ in the pro-rata model, tend to listen to less popular artists. But in streaming this effect is small, regardless of direction.

Years ago, from an audio standpoint, there weren't many Bucs podcasts around. The pinnacle was WTB, and some kinda came and went. I don't believe credentialed media had figured out the podcast market at the time.

Getting into podcasting should always be about exploring an avenue that you're passionate about. It should never be about downloads. It should never be about getting followers or likes on social media. As a podcaster, you should be able to turn on your mic at any time and just go

I was lucky enough to develop good relationships with some credentialed media folks and a few within the Bucs organization. That's the only reason I was allowed to do some of the content I was able to do. We also seemed to have more of a fellowship.

Some others started seeing the trend of podcasting and got into the game. Most were very professional. I helped a few get theirs going, including 1 who would never actually give someone credit and took the route of trashing folks and talking sh!t. Britney would say it was "toxic"

Only speaking for myself, I gravitated toward the type of work I was doing and the content provided by WTB. No matter what crazy was happening, Old School could spell it out for you in a way that people could easily understand. He inhaled the good sh!t and exhaled the bullsh!t.

The trends of social media and trying to be "louder" than others started a trend of dragging down the fanbase. It wasn't team content any longer. It was "how much Scott Reynolds of PR sucks, or "how biased Tom Jones was and you fans should go threaten them at training camp".

Yeah, I legit heard content in an audio format sent to me that suggested to fans that they should harass media members at Bucs training camp. How did the hosting site of this podcast react? They "aren't responsible for the content".

How did the organization react? Well, Hard Knocks was in town, so let's use it as a way to make us look good as an organization and ignore what was being encouraged. IMO, there should have been ZERO tolerance from the organization on this, but yeah,gotta look good for the cameras

I reacted by blocking those individuals -- those who hosted the content, and those who provided it.  Enter a whole slew of new Bucs podcast audio, while in the background, WTB and I are observing what was going on.

And, that content continued to be celebrated. If people wanted to ignore it, they could have, but instead they chose to talk about it, plug it, and allow that ignorance and hate on their own podcasts. Gotta have those clicks and downloads!

I, personally had enough. Too many hours. Too much work. Too many things pulling me away from what was actually important in life, and it wasn't a sport that was important. Sports podcasting is a very interesting topic when it comes to how and who people are invested in.

One of the things I most dislike about living with #mentalhealth problems is how I've become a less good friend & support to others.
Relationships once close become less so or even fade away completely; relationships that could've developed do not do so & also fade away.
That text I didn't send, the call I didn't return, the conversation I didn't have, the visit I didn't make, the thing I didn't do.
While my life stands still, others' move forwards, deepening relationships, forming new ones, while I slip behind, fade away.
People's busy lives & geographical distance mean it takes effort to stay in touch, to make a connection, to be part of others' lives.
Being unable to keep up with relationships could happen with any condition, physical or mental; but it's tricker with #mentalhealth.
People don't really understand the impact living with a #mentalhealth condition can have on your ability to actively maintain relationships.
